column4: The section itself cites this ayah: spouses are reciprocally called لباس, and intimacy is permitted through the fasting night until dawn separates white from black. It joins the section's marital covering to the night/day boundary.

The section's B004 dictionary form غشيان names intercourse as covering; this ayah uses تَغَشَّاهَا for the first couple's union, then says she conceived a light burden. It carries the section's covering image directly into pregnancy.

The next ayah says the child was given, then the parents associated partners with what He gave; فَتَعَالَى اللَّهُ also uses the root ع ل و named for 92:20's الْأَعْلَى. It completes the section's union-to-birth-to-gift sequence with a failure of gratitude.

The section's B003 dictionary form جلاها describes a bride being unveiled and seen; 91:3 uses جَلَّاهَا for daylight disclosing the sun. The shared root and display scene make the section's daylight-as-opening image concrete.

The section names غ ش و for night covering and sexual covering; this ayah uses يَغْشَاهَا for night covering the sun, paired with 91:3's daylight disclosure. It supplies the other half of the section's night/day opposition.

The section names the root غ ش و for covering and joins night/day to a male/female pair; this ayah says يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهَارَ and also speaks of fruits made in pairs. It brings covering and paired creation into one scene.
This ayah calls night a garment (لِبَاسًا) and day a rising/spreading forth. The section's spouses-as-garments image and night/day opening meet in a direct parallel.
The section names the night as what covers; 78:10 says God made night a covering (لِبَاسًا). This is a direct parallel to the opening night image and to the clothing language of 2:187.
This ayah makes day a time of livelihood, completing 78:10's night covering. Its day/night division parallels the section's night that veils and day that opens.
This ayah describes God wrapping night over day and day over night. The reciprocal concealment sharpens the section's paired opposites, where night covers and day appears.
The section's named roots ذ ك ر and ء ن ث occur in the same male/female pair here: خَلَقَ الزَّوْجَيْنِ الذَّكَرَ وَالْأُنثَىٰ. It directly joins paired creation to the section's third ayah.
The next ayah names a drop when it is emitted (نُطْفَةٍ إِذَا تُمْنَىٰ), moving from 53:45's male/female pair to conception, as the section does.
This ayah begins the sequence with an emitted drop (نُطْفَةً مِّن مَّنِيٍّ يُمْنَىٰ). The following verses form it and then name the two sexes, giving another direct conception-to-sex sequence.

The section's B003 dictionary form مخلقة concerns formation of the womb's mudghah; this ayah says the drop becomes a clot and is then created and proportioned (فَخَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ). It bridges 75:37's drop and 75:39's male/female pair.
This ayah says God made from it the two sexes, male and female (الزَّوْجَيْنِ الذَّكَرَ وَالْأُنثَىٰ), directly echoing the section's sex pair after 75:37–38's conception sequence.

The section's B003 dictionary gloss takes مُخَلَّقَةٌ as fully formed flesh in the womb; 22:5 uses مُخَلَّقَةٍ وَغَيْرِ مُخَلَّقَةٍ for a womb-lump. It anchors the shared root while preserving the ayah's contrast between formed and unformed.
This ayah names a مُّضْغَةً and describes its development into bones clothed with flesh. It is a direct Quranic womb scene for the section's dictionary discussion of mudghah and formation.
This ayah describes creation after creation inside mothers' wombs, within three layers of darkness. It joins the section's hidden, covering night image to gestation and formation.

This ayah says God knows what every female carries (مَا تَحْمِلُ كُلُّ أُنثَىٰ) and what wombs decrease or increase. It expands the section's birth scene and its 3:36 line that God knows what the mother delivered.

This ayah joins creation from a drop to being made pairs, then says no female conceives or gives birth outside God's knowledge. It makes the section's male/female pair, conception, birth, and divine giving one connected account.
This ayah says God created humans in pairs (أَزْوَاجًا), directly paralleling the section's pairing of night/day and male/female and its claim that God creates both sexes.

The ayah names creation from male and female (ذَكَرٍ وَأُنثَىٰ), then locates honor with God in taqwa. It directly meets the section's reversal of a value scale that ranked a boy's birth above a girl's.

This ayah says God gives daughters and sons to whom He wills (يَهَبُ ... إِنَاثًا ... الذُّكُورَ). It treats both sexes as gifts, undoing the birth formula that assigned ease to boys and hardship to girls.

This ayah completes 42:49 by adding mixed pairs of sons and daughters and those made barren. Its own contribution is to place sex and childlessness within what God gives or withholds, as the section does.

The section explicitly distinguishes the root ص د ق's mahr branch from 92:6's “affirm”; this ayah commands, وَآتُوا النِّسَاءَ صَدُقَاتِهِنَّ. It is the direct Quranic wording for the bride's dower as something given to her.

The section names the root خ ل ق for the formed womb-lump; this ayah says God created the human from a drop and proportioned him (خَلَقَهُ فَقَدَّرَهُ). It connects embryonic origin with measured creation.

The section cites 92:7's ease and links birth's exit to life's path; this ayah says God made the path easy (السَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُ). The shared ease root gives the section's birth/path connection a Quranic counterpart.

The ayah measures a pregnant woman's waiting period by delivery (أَن يَضَعْنَ حَمْلَهُنَّ), then promises ease for whoever is mindful of God (يُسْرًا). It directly joins childbirth to ease and taqwa, as the section's 92:5–10 contrast does.

This ayah says a mother carries and gives birth with hardship (كُرْهًا) and makes that labor part of the call to gratitude toward parents. It supplies the bodily cost behind the section's difficult-birth dictionary sense.
This ayah describes a mother carrying her child in weakness upon weakness and weaning him in two years. It gives the section's birth-and-hardship image a second, sustained account of maternal burden.
The section recalls the wife of Imran dedicating what is in her womb (مَا فِي بَطْنِي) to God; this ayah is that vow. It sets the expected child's birth inside an act of offering.
The section quotes the mother saying وَضَعْتُهَا أُنثَىٰ and the Quran's reply that God knows what she bore. This ayah's own words name the newborn girl and place the birth within divine knowledge.
This ayah says her Lord accepted Mary with good acceptance (بِقَبُولٍ حَسَنٍ), completing 3:36's birth of a girl. That acceptance reverses the social devaluation the section sets beside female birth.

This ayah describes humanity created from one soul and its mate, then spread as many men and women. It is a broader creation-and-couple parallel to the first couple in 7:189 and the paired sexes in the section.

This ayah says God made spouses from among people so they may find tranquility in one another, with affection and mercy between them. It adds the relational purpose of the bride-and-husband union developed in the section.

This ayah praises the Creator of pairs in what the earth grows, in human selves, and in what people do not know. It broadens the section's specific night/day and male/female pairs into a Quranic theme of paired creation.

This ayah connects spouses made from among people with sons and grandchildren and with provision. It supplies a household sequence—pairing, offspring, provision—that complements the section's bride, birth, and gift images.

The section's B004 dictionary wording أتيته (“I came to that place”) is offered as a euphemism for intercourse; this ayah uses فَأْتُوا in its marital intercourse instruction and places it beside fertility imagery. It makes the section's “coming” euphemism concrete in a reproductive setting.

This ayah says the people assign daughters to God while keeping what they desire for themselves. It sets the gendered preference that 16:58 shows on a father's face, the same value scale the section overturns.

This ayah says a man darkens when told of a female child (بِالْأُنثَىٰ ... مُسْوَدًّا). The section explicitly likens that darkness on the face to night and names the same female-birth word, exposing the valuation it later dissolves.
This ayah completes 16:58: the father weighs keeping the girl in disgrace against burying her in the ground. That is the concrete harm behind the section's rejected ranking of male and female birth.

This ayah asks whether God took daughters from what He creates while choosing sons for the people. It repeats the gendered assignment exposed in 16:57 and makes the section's male/female valuation a boundary of its own.

This ayah repeats the face darkening and swallowed grief when one is given news of what he assigns to the Most Merciful; 43:16 identifies that as daughters. The repeated scene reinforces the section's image of gender bias darkening a face.

This ayah asks whether the male is for the people and the female for God (الذَّكَرُ ... الْأُنثَىٰ). Its own context concerns the assignment of divine beings, not human children, but the same unequal male/female valuation is directly challenged.
This ayah calls that allocation an unjust division (قِسْمَةٌ ضِيزَىٰ), completing 53:21. It gives a Quranic judgment on the same asymmetry the section exposes in the preference for sons.
This ayah names the buried-alive girl (الْمَوْءُودَةُ), the stark endpoint of the section's account of devaluing daughters at birth. The following ayah asks for what sin she was killed.
This ayah asks the buried girl for what sin she was killed (بِأَيِّ ذَنبٍ قُتِلَتْ), completing 81:8. It makes the section's reversal of the male-over-female birth measure a direct moral boundary.

The section gives the root ه د ي a bridal dictionary sense, “the bride was led to her husband”; this ayah uses يَهْدِيهِمْ for God's guidance along paths of peace and out of darkness into light. The bridge is modest because the ayah describes spiritual guidance, while the section activates the root's concrete sense of leading someone to a destination.
